Where it began

Abdul Razzaq was born on 2 December 1979 in Shahdara Bagh, on the edge of Lahore. Watching Wasim Akram made him want to bowl fast, and he took to the craft early: on Pakistan's Under-19 tour of the West Indies in 1996 he took 17 wickets and chipped in with the bat.

Later that year, a month short of his seventeenth birthday, he played his first one-day international, against Zimbabwe at the Gaddafi Stadium in his home city. His first Test followed three years on, against Australia in Brisbane in November 1999.

The player

He played 46 Tests between 1999 and 2006, scoring 1,946 runs at 28.62 with three hundreds, the best of them 134 against Bangladesh in Dhaka, and taking 100 wickets at 36.93. That put him among the few Pakistanis to reach the double of 1,000 runs and 100 wickets. His best Test bowling, 5 for 35, came against Sri Lanka in Karachi.

In 2000, aged 20, he took a Test hat-trick against Sri Lanka at Galle, the youngest bowler to that point to manage one. In one-day cricket he was an even bigger presence: 265 matches, three hundreds, a place in the side that reached the 1999 World Cup final and in the team that won the World Twenty20 in 2009, where his 3 for 20 helped win the final.

What made him special

He was a rare mix. With the ball he was accurate and canny, moving it both ways, hiding a leg-cutter and, at his best, reversing the old ball at around 140 km/h. With the bat he could either flatten an attack or dig in for hours. Against India at Mohali in 2005 he batted for nearly six hours alongside Kamran Akmal to save a Test, scoring 46 from 183 balls.

That patience surprised people who knew him for hitting. In 2005 a poll of leading bowlers placed him ninth among the batsmen they most feared in one-day cricket, one spot ahead of Ricky Ponting. He is also the only man to have batted in every position from opener to number eleven in ODIs, which suggests captains were never quite sure where to put him, and that he never minded.

Away from the middle

He was popular in English county cricket too, with spells at Middlesex, Worcestershire, Surrey, Hampshire and Leicestershire, and he was on the winning side at T20 finals day with both Hampshire and Leicestershire. After playing he turned to coaching, with a keen interest in teaching power-hitting. As head coach of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa he led them to the Quaid-e-Azam Trophy, the National T20 Cup and the Pakistan Cup in the 2020–21 season, and he later worked with the national team.

And finally

In a one-day series in Australia in 2000 he hit Glenn McGrath for five fours in a row. New Zealand's captain Stephen Fleming once called him the best hitter in the world. McGrath may not have needed persuading.
